paper_title: Judge-dependent safety gains and model-specific helpfulness costs of evidence-sufficiency prompting in clinical LLMs
core_problem: Whether measured 'safety gains' from evidence-sufficiency prompting in clinical LLMs reflect real behavior change or are artifacts of the LLM judge's calibration, and what the associated helpfulness costs are.
methodology_summary: Retrospective public-data benchmark using a fully paired common panel (1,200 cells) comparing a standard prompt against an evidence-sufficiency wrapper across four models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Grok 4.3). Primary endpoint was paired reduction in unsafe overconfidence scored by GPT-5.4-nano, with secondary analyses involving other judges and blinded clinician review.
empirical_results: Unsafe overconfidence reduced from 49.3% to 24.7% (24.7 point paired reduction, p<0.001). The magnitude of the gain was judge-dependent (e.g., Claude Sonnet halved the effect). The gain carried a model-specific helpfulness cost (e.g., near-free for GPT-5.5, near-total for Gemini). Matched scaffold controls showed genuine behavior change.
explicit_limitations: The study is a retrospective public-data benchmark and perturbation study with paired repeated measures. No established reporting guideline covers non-interventional computational benchmarks of clinical LLM behavior. The findings do not establish clinical deployment readiness.
